draft.title: Enzyme inhibitors
card: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a reaction. The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on. It binds at a region of the enzyme called the active site.
An enzyme inhibitor is a molecule that slows or stops an enzyme. Many medicines work this way.
A competitive inhibitor has a shape and charge pattern that fit the active site. It binds there, so the real substrate cannot bind while the inhibitor is in place.
With the enzyme blocked, its reaction slows. If that reaction is needed by a bacterium or a virus, the medicine can help stop the infection.
draft.remember: An inhibitor medicine blocks the active site, so the substrate cannot bind and the reaction slows.

a.q: How does a competitive inhibitor medicine reduce the rate of an enzyme's reaction?
opts: It binds to the active site and blocks the substrate
It joins the substrate and turns it into a product
It lowers the temperature of the enzyme's surroundings
It adds more substrate for the enzyme to act on
a.why: The inhibitor fits the active site, so the substrate has no place to bind and the reaction slows. The enzyme is not helped by extra substrate, because the site is taken by the inhibitor.
a.clue: Think about what sits in the active site.

b.q: A drug designed by a chemist in Geelong has a shape that fits the active site of a viral enzyme. What is the most likely effect on that enzyme?
opts: The viral substrate cannot bind, so the reaction slows
The viral substrate binds faster, so the reaction speeds up
The enzyme is changed into a different substrate
The enzyme's primary structure is rebuilt as a new protein
b.why: A drug that fits the active site occupies it, so the viral substrate cannot bind and the reaction slows. It does not speed the reaction up, because a bound inhibitor blocks the substrate rather than helping it.
b.clue: What happens to the substrate when the active site is already occupied?

a.best: It binds to the active site and blocks the substrate

b.best: The viral substrate cannot bind, so the reaction slows

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'The enzyme is not helped by extra substrate, because the site is taken by the inhibitor.' This is false for competitive inhibition. Raising substrate concentration can outcompete the inhibitor and restore the rate, which is the defining feature of a competitive inhibitor.
The first bullet defines an enzyme as a protein that speeds up a reaction. That definition belongs to point 4 (Enzymes) and should only be mentioned here, not explained.

The remember line says 'An inhibitor medicine blocks the active site', which applies it to all inhibitors. The card limits active-site blocking to competitive inhibitors, and the chapter says only 'some medicines' do this. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere.

check.summary: Why (a) wrongly says extra substrate cannot help, but competitive inhibition can be overcome by more substrate. The card also re-defines 'enzyme' from point 4, and the remember line applies active-site blocking to all inhibitor medicines rather than only competitive ones.
